description: Predict visible passes of a satellite (e.g. the ISS, NORAD 25544) over an observer in the next `days`. Identify the satellite by exactly one of `norad_id` or `name` — supplying both, or neither, is rejected. A few well-known common names resolve directly to their catalog numbers, ignoring case: ISS or International Space Station (25544), Hubble, Hubble Space Telescope, or HST (20580), and Tiangong, CSS, or Chinese Space Station (48274). Any other `name` is matched as a case-insensitive substring of CelesTrak's catalog names, so it resolves only when it picks out a single object: a broader query comes back with the matching objects and their catalog numbers to choose from. Either way the result echoes the query that resolved it as `resolved_from_name`. Fetches the object's current GP element set from CelesTrak, propagates it with SGP4 in-process, and returns each pass's rise, peak, and set times with azimuths and the peak elevation, plus the stretch of the pass visible to the naked eye: `visible_start_utc` through `visible_end_utc`, with the elevation and azimuth at each end. A pass is returned when that visible stretch — the satellite above the horizon and sunlit while the Sun is below −6° for the observer — reaches 10° elevation, wherever in the pass it falls. `sunlit` reports illumination at the peak instant, so it is false on a pass seen only before it enters Earth's shadow or after it leaves. Rise, set, and the visible-stretch edges are within 1 s of the true instants; the peak is the highest sample of a 30-second scan. Every returned pass rises in the requested window or in the 30 s before `start`: a pass up longer than that at `start` is omitted rather than reported with `start` as its rise, so back up `start` to see it, while a pass still up when the window ends is reported through its actual set. Searches at most 10 days per call: a larger `days`, up to 30, searches the first 10 and returns a notice naming the exact `start` and `days` that continue the search with no pass repeated or skipped, while that start stays within about a month of the element set's epoch. A `start` further than about a month from the element set's epoch is rejected as out of range on that distance alone, and an element set that will not propagate to a window inside that horizon is rejected as a reentry — so an empty `passes` means only that nothing was visible. CelesTrak publishes only current element sets, so in practice `start` must be within about a month of today. NORAD catalog numbers and catalog names are found at celestrak.org or heavens-above.com. This is a gated, network-backed extension (CelesTrak is keyless but rate-limited; element sets are cached briefly). Default elevation 0 m; pass an IANA timezone for observer-local pass times.

days.description: Number of days ahead to search for passes. Default 7. At most 10 are searched per call; a value up to 30 searches the first 10 with a notice naming the `start` and `days` that continue the search.

elevation.description: Observer elevation in meters above sea level. Default 0.

latitude.description: Observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive.

longitude.description: Observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive.

name.description: Satellite name to resolve, e.g. "ISS (ZARYA)". The common names ISS, International Space Station, Hubble, Hubble Space Telescope, HST, Tiangong, CSS, and Chinese Space Station resolve directly to their catalog numbers, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. Any other name is matched against CelesTrak as a case-insensitive substring of the catalog name, so give the fullest name you have — a short one matches many objects and is rejected as ambiguous. Mutually exclusive with `norad_id` — supply exactly one.

norad_id.description: NORAD catalog number of the satellite, e.g. 25544 for the ISS. Found at celestrak.org or heavens-above.com. Mutually exclusive with `name` — supply exactly one.

start.description: Search start as an ISO 8601 UTC string, within about a month of the current element set's epoch — for a tracked object that epoch is hours old, so in practice within about a month of today. A start further out is rejected rather than answered from elements that no longer describe the orbit. Defaults to now. A value with no zone designator is read as UTC, not the local zone of the server process.

timezone.description: IANA timezone for localized pass times, e.g. "America/Los_Angeles". When omitted, output is UTC-only.

name: astronomy_get_satellite_passes

error.description: Present when the call failed. Absent on success.

code.description: JSON-RPC error code for this failure.

reason.description: Machine-readable failure mode. Declared by this tool: `invalid_time`: The start timestamp is not a parseable ISO 8601 instant, or names a calendar date that does not exist (e.g. 2026-02-30). `time_out_of_range`: The start instant falls outside the years 1900–2100, or more than about a month from the epoch of the current element set — checked on the epoch distance itself, since SGP4 keeps returning positions well past the point where the mean elements describe the orbit. `invalid_timezone`: The `timezone` value is not an IANA zone this runtime knows. `invalid_target`: Neither `norad_id` nor `name` was supplied, or both were. `tle_not_found`: CelesTrak has no current element set for the NORAD ID. `satellite_name_not_found`: No current CelesTrak object has a name containing the `name` value. `ambiguous_satellite_name`: The `name` value matches more than one current object and none of them carries it as their whole name. The error names the match count and lists the matching objects with their catalog numbers, capped when there are more than the list holds. A capped list carries a hint leading with narrowing instead of with the list, since the wanted object need not be among the ones shown. `object_decayed`: A current element set will not propagate to a window near its own epoch — the signature of an object that has reentered. `celestrak_unavailable`: The element-set fetch failed after retries, or returned a body that is not JSON at all. `malformed_element_set`: CelesTrak answered with parsable JSON whose GP record does not carry the fields an OMM element set requires — a permanent property of that record, not the transient outage celestrak_unavailable covers. The same request returns the same record, so retrying it can only fail again. Other values are possible when a failure originates below the handler.

recovery.description: Actionable next step for the caller.

message.description: Human-readable description of what went wrong.

norad_id.description: The NORAD catalog number echoed from the request.

notice.description: How to search the days the per-call cap held back: the exact `start` and `days` to re-call with, or — when that start would lie more than about a month from the element set's epoch — that no call can search them. Absent when every requested day was searched.

passes.description: Passes whose visible stretch — the satellite above the horizon and sunlit while the Sun is below −6° for the observer — reaches 10° elevation, in the window searched, chronological.

items.description: One visible pass: horizon-to-horizon rise/peak/set geometry, illumination at peak, and the stretch of the pass that is visible to the naked eye.

duration_seconds.description: Pass duration from `rise_utc` to `set_utc`, in seconds.

peak_altitude_degrees.description: Maximum elevation angle during the pass, in degrees, as sampled every 30 seconds.

peak_azimuth_degrees.description: Azimuth at peak elevation, in degrees.

peak_local.description: Peak time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

peak_utc.description: Time of maximum elevation in ISO 8601 UTC, the highest sample of a 30-second scan.

rise_local.description: Rise time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

rise_utc.description: Rise above the horizon in ISO 8601 UTC, within 1 s of the true crossing. Can fall up to 30 s before `start` when the satellite rose inside the 30-second scan step ending at `start`.

set_local.description: Set time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

set_utc.description: Set below the horizon in ISO 8601 UTC, within 1 s of the true crossing.

sunlit.description: True when the satellite is in sunlight at the peak instant. False on a pass that enters Earth's shadow before its peak or leaves it after — the visible_* fields say when it can be seen.

visible_end_altitude_degrees.description: Elevation where the visible stretch ends, in degrees — 0 when it ends at the set.

visible_end_azimuth_degrees.description: Azimuth where the visible stretch ends, in degrees.

visible_end_local.description: Visible-stretch end in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

visible_end_utc.description: End of the visible stretch in ISO 8601 UTC. Equals `set_utc` when the pass is visible until it sets; otherwise within 1 s of the moment it enters Earth's shadow or the sky brightens.

visible_start_altitude_degrees.description: Elevation where the visible stretch starts, in degrees — 0 when it starts at the rise.

visible_start_azimuth_degrees.description: Azimuth where the visible stretch starts, in degrees — where to look first.

visible_start_local.description: Visible-stretch start in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

visible_start_utc.description: Start of the visible stretch — above the horizon, sunlit, over a dark sky — in ISO 8601 UTC. Equals `rise_utc` when the pass is visible from its rise; otherwise within 1 s of the moment it leaves Earth's shadow or the sky darkens.

resolved_from_name.description: The name query that resolved this object. Present only when the request supplied `name` rather than `norad_id`.

satellite_name.description: Satellite name as CelesTrak catalogs it (the element set's OBJECT_NAME).

totalCount.description: Number of visible passes found in the window searched.

title: astronomy-mcp-server: get satellite passes
